title: Design a URL Shortener
subtitle: Design key generation, redirect storage, caching, partitioning, and analytics
objectives: Turn a vague prompt into requirements and back-of-envelope numbers
Design the key generation scheme, and defend it against the obvious alternatives
Apply the read-heavy playbook: caching, replicas, and where the truth lives
Handle the real edges: collisions, custom aliases, expiry, and analytics at scale

exercises.title: Requirements and workload estimates define the design envelope
exercises.body: Convert the prompt into functional requirements, latency and availability targets, average and peak request rates, read:write ratio, record size, and retention period. These inputs determine throughput and storage bounds before any component is selected.
exercises.note: Designing from averages alone can hide a peak-load bottleneck; record both sustained and burst traffic when capacity changes with either.

exercises.prompt: A redirect service sends every lookup to a database capped at 10,000 reads/s while traffic reaches 116,000 reads/s. Cache 95% of mappings.
exercises.result: Hot redirects stopped reaching the database
exercises.why: A 95% hit rate leaves 5% of 116,000 requests, or 5,800 reads/s, for the link store. Expiration, deletion, and abuse disabling still require cache invalidation or bounded TTLs.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A redirect service sends every lookup to a database capped at 10,000 reads/s while traffic reaches 116,000 reads/s. Cache 95% of mappings. Place Mapping cache, Link store. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Redirects → Mapping cache; Mapping cache → Link store. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A 95% hit rate leaves 5% of 116,000 requests, or 5,800 reads/s, for the link store. Expiration, deletion, and abuse disabling still require cache invalidation or bounded TTLs.

exercises.prompt: 'Design a URL shortener.' What's the first move?
choices: Choose a database
Pin down requirements and scale: what must it do, how many writes, how many reads, and what's the read:write ratio
Draw the architecture
Pick a hashing algorithm
exercises.why: Traffic volume, read-to-write ratio, record size, retention, and latency targets determine which resources can become bottlenecks. In particular, a high read-to-write ratio favors spending capacity on the redirect path and evaluating caches or read replicas before optimizing link creation.

exercises.prompt: Which are the core functional requirements? Select all.
choices: Given a long URL, return a short one
Given a short URL, redirect to the long one
Links may expire
Real-time collaborative editing of links
exercises.why: The stated product requires creating a short mapping, resolving it during redirect, and optionally expiring it. Collaborative editing introduces permissions, concurrent updates, and versioning without supporting any stated requirement, so it should not shape this design.

exercises.prompt: 100 million new links per day averages about 1,160 writes/sec. A 5× peak is about 5,800 writes/sec. What does this estimate imply?
choices: The write path requires global sharding immediately
A well-tuned database can plausibly handle the write rate; measure peaks before adding write complexity
Redirect reads will also be 5,800/sec
Each application server should keep its own link database
exercises.why: An estimated peak of 5,800 writes/sec is within the plausible range of a well-tuned database for small records, subject to measured storage and durability costs. The estimate does not justify global sharding by itself; it identifies redirect reads and long-term storage as separate dimensions to size.

exercises.prompt: Reads are 100× writes. So ~116,000 redirects/second. What does that ratio tell you about the design?
choices: You need to shard immediately
It's overwhelmingly a read system — so caching and replicas carry the design, and the write path can stay simple
You need a NoSQL database
You need multiple regions
exercises.why: At 100 redirects per link creation, read-path work is repeated far more often than write-path work. Reducing each redirect to a cache or indexed key lookup yields more capacity benefit than optimizing an already less frequent creation request.

exercises.prompt: At 500 bytes per record, the system adds about 50 GB/day, 18 TB/year, and 91 TB over five years before replication and indexes. Which conclusion follows?
choices: The data will always fit on one ordinary server
Storage partitioning may be needed over the retention period, even though the write rate is moderate
The redirect path needs no cache
Every record should be copied into application memory
exercises.why: A 91 TB primary dataset exceeds the practical local storage of many single database hosts, and replicas and indexes increase the physical footprint further. The moderate write rate and the large retained dataset are different constraints, so capacity planning should include partitioning or distributed storage without assuming the write path is overloaded.

exercises.prompt: Your estimates say ~1,200 writes/sec and ~91TB over five years. What have you learned?
choices: You need a massive distributed system
Writes are easy and storage is the growth problem — so the design questions are the read path and how the data is partitioned over time, not write throughput
One server is enough
You need to shard by user
exercises.why: The supplied estimates show a moderate creation rate and a much larger long-term storage footprint. That combination supports a simple write path initially while requiring a key and storage layout that can be partitioned as retained mappings accumulate.

exercises.title: Link creation is a conditional insert, not a hash function
exercises.body: The client sends `POST /links` with a destination URL. The service validates it, generates a candidate code, and attempts `INSERT(short_code, destination_url)`. A unique constraint is the authority on whether the code is free. A conflict generates another candidate; a successful commit returns the short URL.
exercises.note: The generator proposes a code; the database proves uniqueness. Random generation needs collision retries. Allocated counters avoid collisions but add coordination and make codes easier to enumerate.

exercises.prompt: Build the complete creation path for one short link. A concurrent writer may choose the same candidate code.
steps: Validate the destination URL and creation policy
Attempt to insert `short_code → destination_url` under a unique constraint
If the insert conflicts, generate another candidate and retry within a bounded attempt budget
After the insert commits, return `201 Created` with the short URL
exercises.why: Validation precedes allocation so invalid or forbidden destinations consume no mapping. The insert—not an earlier read—is the uniqueness decision because two creators can observe an empty code simultaneously. Returning only after commit prevents issuing a short URL whose mapping does not exist.

exercises.prompt: Match each field in the authoritative link record to why the creation or redirect path needs it.

pairs.right: Enforces uniqueness and serves the redirect lookup
The value returned by a successful code lookup
Authorizes management without changing redirect identity
Lets resolution reject a mapping after its validity window

exercises.why: The redirect path is a primary-key lookup from `short_code` to `destination_url`, optionally checking expiry. Ownership belongs in the same authoritative record for management operations, while high-volume click events belong on an asynchronous analytics path rather than this hot row.

exercises.prompt: A 7-character code using letters and digits provides about 3.5 trillion possible codes. At 100 million new links per day, five years adds about 183 billion links. What does this imply?
choices: The code space is too small within the first year
The code space has substantial headroom, but uniqueness still must be enforced
Every generated code will be unique without a database constraint
The code must encode the creation date
exercises.why: Five years of links would consume roughly 183 billion of 3.5 trillion possible codes, leaving substantial address-space headroom. Capacity does not guarantee uniqueness: random generation can still choose an occupied code, so insertion needs a unique constraint and retry behavior.

exercises.prompt: Approach A: hash the long URL (say MD5) and take the first 7 characters. What's the problem?
choices: Hashing is too slow
Truncating a hash produces collisions — two different URLs can map to the same 7 characters, so you must detect that and handle it on every write
MD5 is insecure for this
The output isn't URL-safe
exercises.why: Truncating a hash maps many possible URLs into a finite code space, so distinct URLs can produce the same short code. The write path must detect an occupied code and derive a different candidate, for example by adding a salt or counter before hashing again.

exercises.prompt: Approach B: use an auto-incrementing counter and encode the number in base62. What does that buy?
choices: Nothing over hashing
No collisions ever, by construction — each number is used once, and base62 just changes how you write it down
Shorter codes
Better security
exercises.why: An atomic counter assigns each link a distinct integer, and base62 encoding only represents that integer with letters and digits. Because different counter values encode to different strings, the generator avoids random collisions while the counter remains unique.

exercises.prompt: What are the real downsides of the counter approach? Select all.
choices: Codes are sequential, so anyone can enumerate every link ever created
It reveals roughly how many links you've made — a business metric you may not want public
A single global counter is a coordination point that must be unique across all servers
It produces collisions
exercises.why: Adjacent counter values produce enumerable codes, allowing a scraper to discover mappings by walking the sequence and infer creation volume. The shared counter also requires coordination across writers; collision risk is absent because the counter provides distinct values.

exercises.prompt: So how do you get a counter without every write hitting one coordination point?
choices: Use a random number instead
Hand each server a pre-allocated range — server A gets 1–10,000, B gets 10,001–20,000 — so servers only coordinate once per block, not once per link
Use a timestamp
Let each server keep its own counter
exercises.why: Allocating a disjoint block of IDs lets each server generate many codes locally after one coordinated reservation. This reduces counter contention and round trips, while a crashed server can leave unused gaps; gaps do not violate uniqueness.

exercises.prompt: Your product promises that secret links resist discovery without authorization. Slide toward your key scheme.
exercises.rightLabel: 128-bit random token + rate limits (longer, far harder to guess)
exercises.why: Seven base62 characters provide about 3.5 trillion values, but after 183 billion links exist a random guess hits an occupied code about 5% of the time. A secret link therefore needs a high-entropy capability token, such as at least 128 random bits, plus rate limiting; sensitive resources should also require authorization because obscurity alone is not access control.

exercises.title: Immutable key-value mappings support a cache-first redirect path
exercises.body: For `GET /{code}`, the service looks up the code in a cache. On a miss, it reads the key-value store, caches the long URL, and returns the redirect. Repeated requests for a hot code terminate at the cache and consume no database read capacity.
exercises.note: If destinations become editable, cached mappings require invalidation or versioning; otherwise redirects can continue serving an old destination.

exercises.prompt: Redirects wait 320ms because every click writes analytics before returning the destination. Keep redirect latency independent of analytics processing.
exercises.result: The redirect path now performs only the work required to send the user onward
exercises.why: The redirect response needs the destination mapping, not a completed analytics write. A durable queue removes analytics latency from the user path. The worker must tolerate duplicate events because queue delivery may repeat.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: Redirects wait 320ms because every click writes analytics before returning the destination. Keep redirect latency independent of analytics processing. Place Redirect API, Click queue, Analytics worker. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Browser → Redirect API; Redirect API → Click queue; Click queue → Analytics worker. That topology is the evidence for the answer: The redirect response needs the destination mapping, not a completed analytics write. A durable queue removes analytics latency from the user path. The worker must tolerate duplicate events because queue delivery may repeat.

exercises.prompt: 116,000 redirects/sec, and the same popular links are requested constantly. Add the piece that absorbs that read load.
exercises.why: Short-code mappings are small, read frequently, and usually immutable, while request popularity is often skewed toward a limited set of links. A cache can serve those hot mappings without a database read, leaving the database authoritative for misses.

exercises.prompt: Why are these mappings unusually good cache candidates?
choices: They're small
Generated destinations normally stay fixed, so update invalidation is rare; expiry, deletion, or abuse disabling still needs a TTL, invalidation, or tombstone
They're requested rarely
They're stored as text
exercises.why: Generated destinations are normally immutable, so ordinary reads do not create update-driven staleness. The cache still needs a correctness policy for expiry, deletion, and abuse disabling: use a bounded time to live (TTL), explicit invalidation, or a cached tombstone so a disabled code does not keep redirecting.

exercises.prompt: Should the redirect return 301 (permanent) or 302 (temporary)?
choices: 301 always — the mapping is permanent
It's a tradeoff: a cacheable 301 can let later navigations bypass the shortener, reducing load but making server-side click counts incomplete
302 always — it's safer
It doesn't matter
exercises.why: A browser may cache a `301 Moved Permanently` response and redirect future visits without contacting the shortener, reducing server traffic but hiding those visits from server-side analytics. A `302 Found` response usually preserves more requests for measurement at the cost of serving more redirect traffic.

exercises.prompt: Your cache holds the hot links. A brand-new viral link is created and instantly gets 50,000 requests/second. What happens?
choices: The cache serves it
The first requests all miss simultaneously and stampede the database for the same key — a thundering herd on one row
The database rejects them
The link is rate limited
exercises.why: Concurrent misses for one newly popular code can send identical queries to the database. Per-process request coalescing allows one fetch while local requests wait, reducing the load to roughly one query per application process; a shared lease or shielding tier is needed to coordinate across processes.

exercises.prompt: Which database fits this workload?
choices: It must be relational for the transactions
Almost anything: the access pattern is a key-value lookup by short code, so a KV store fits perfectly — and it's the access pattern, not fashion, that says so
It must be NoSQL for the scale
A graph database
exercises.why: The redirect path performs a point lookup from short code to long URL, which matches a key-value store's primary access pattern. A relational database can also serve this indexed lookup; the key-value choice is justified when joins and ad hoc relational queries are not required.

exercises.prompt: How would you shard 91TB of links?
choices: By creation date
By hash of the short code — every redirect supplies that lookup key, so the router can select one shard
By long URL
By user id
exercises.why: Every redirect supplies the short code, so hashing that code routes the lookup to one shard without a scatter-gather query. Sharding by creation date can concentrate new writes, and sharding by creator requires information the redirect request may not contain.

exercises.title: Generated codes, custom aliases, and routes share one namespace
exercises.body: The redirect key is the namespace identifier regardless of who chose it. Generated codes and user aliases therefore need one atomic uniqueness constraint. Application routes such as `/api` must be excluded from allocation through a reserved-key or reserved-prefix set.
exercises.note: Separate allocation paths without a shared uniqueness check can accept the same key concurrently and make redirect behavior depend on write order.

exercises.prompt: A user wants the custom alias `/launch`. How does that interact with your generated keys?
choices: Keep them in separate systems
They share one namespace, so a custom alias can collide with a generated one — you need a uniqueness constraint over both, and generated keys ideally shouldn't land on nice words
Custom aliases can't be supported
Generate the custom alias by hashing it
exercises.why: Custom aliases and generated codes share one key namespace, so concurrent claims require an atomic uniqueness constraint. Reserving prefixes or using a separate generated-code alphabet can reduce conflicts, but the storage layer must still reject duplicate keys.

exercises.prompt: Links can expire. How do you delete 100 million expired links a day?
choices: A nightly DELETE query across the table
Don't delete on read paths — either let the store expire them by TTL, or sweep in small batches, because one enormous DELETE will lock and lag everything
Delete them as they're requested
Never delete them
exercises.why: Deleting millions of expired rows in one transaction can hold locks, generate a large write-ahead log, and delay replicas. Store-managed time to live (TTL), meaning automatic expiration after a deadline, or small idempotent batches bounds each cleanup operation and permits safe retries.

exercises.prompt: Build the click-analytics path so 116,000 redirects/sec do not wait for aggregation.
exercises.why: The redirect service emits a small event to the queue, workers aggregate events in batches, and the analytics store serves totals without joining the redirect path. If workers fail, durable queued events can wait and replay; writing analytics synchronously would let a slow or unavailable analytics store delay or fail redirects.

exercises.prompt: Which guarantees belong on the link-creation path? Select all.
choices: Atomic uniqueness: only one mapping can claim a code
Global linearizability for click counters
Read-your-writes: the creator can resolve the code they just created
Instantly consistent analytics in every region
exercises.why: A storage uniqueness constraint atomically prevents two destinations from claiming one code. Immediate creator visibility is a read-your-writes session guarantee, which can be provided by routing that creator's read to the write authority or a caught-up replica; it does not require global linearizability for every reader. Click totals and dashboards can usually lag without changing redirect correctness.

exercises.prompt: Someone shortens a malicious URL and it spreads. What have you built without meaning to?
choices: Nothing — you just store strings
An anonymizer: your trusted domain now launders links whose destination nobody can see before clicking
A caching problem
A rate limiting problem
exercises.why: A short URL conceals its destination before the click, which attackers can exploit for phishing or malware delivery. Destination blocklists, creation rate limits, abuse reporting, and an optional preview page reduce that risk and must be part of the service requirements.

exercises.prompt: Summarize the design in one line.
choices: A distributed database with complex sharding
A key-value lookup that's overwhelmingly read-heavy and immutable — so the design is a cache in front of a KV store, and the interesting decisions are key generation, analytics, and abuse
A microservices architecture with a message bus
A relational database with heavy indexing
exercises.why: The design follows from the workload: moderate creation traffic uses a durable uniqueness-enforcing write path, high redirect traffic uses cached point lookups, and immutable mappings minimize invalidation. Key generation, asynchronous analytics, expiration, and abuse controls address the main correctness and operational risks.

exercises.title: Creation and redirect share one authoritative mapping but have different workloads
exercises.body: Creation validates a destination and commits one unique `short_code → destination_url` mapping. Redirect performs a cache-first lookup of that mapping and returns immediately; click analytics leaves through a queue. The database owns correctness, while cache and analytics are derived paths.
exercises.note: A newly committed code needs read-your-writes behavior. Populate or invalidate its cache key after commit, or route the creator's immediate lookup to an authority that can observe the write.

exercises.prompt: Creation checks `SELECT short_code` and sees no row, then inserts. Two concurrent requests both pass the check and claim `/launch` for different destinations.
choices: Check twice before inserting
Add `UNIQUE(short_code)` and treat one insert conflict as failure or retry
Let the last insert overwrite the first
choiceFeedback: Two requests can still interleave after both checks.
The storage constraint serializes the claim at the only point that can decide it atomically.
Overwrite changes an already-issued link's destination and violates mapping identity.
exercises.beforeStatus: ALIAS /launch · two successful creators · destination overwritten
exercises.afterStatus: ALIAS /launch · one committed owner · one conflict response
exercises.result: Exactly one mapping claims the code
exercises.why: A preflight read and a later write are a check-then-act race. The unique constraint places observation and claim inside one atomic storage operation, so custom aliases fail clearly while random-code creation can generate another candidate and retry.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Creation checks `SELECT short_code` and sees no row, then inserts. Two concurrent requests both pass the check and claim `/launch` for different destinations. Place UNIQUE code. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Creator A → UNIQUE code; Creator B → UNIQUE code. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A preflight read and a later write are a check-then-act race. The unique constraint places observation and claim inside one atomic storage operation, so custom aliases fail clearly while random-code creation can generate another candidate and retry.

exercises.prompt: Build the complete hot redirect path while keeping click analytics off the response path.
exercises.why: The cache answers hot lookups, the mapping store repairs misses, and the queue accepts click events without making redirect latency depend on aggregation. A synchronous analytics database would put an optional write on the critical path.

exercises.prompt: A design review finds deterministic hashing of only the destination URL, no unique constraint, mutable destinations cached forever, and synchronous click writes. Which failures follow? Select all.
choices: Different owners cannot receive independent links for the same destination
A collision can bind one code to the wrong destination
Edits or abuse disabling can remain stale indefinitely
Analytics failure can delay or fail redirects
exercises.why: Each finding breaks a separate requirement: destination-only identity collapses distinct creation intents, missing uniqueness permits conflicting ownership, unbounded caching ignores mapping changes, and synchronous analytics couples optional processing to the redirect's latency and availability.

exercises.prompt: A webhook service gives each registered callback a short public ID. Two clients concurrently request the same custom ID. What must choose the winner?
choices: Whichever request has lower latency according to the client
The cache
An atomic unique insert in authoritative storage
A prior unlocked SELECT
exercises.why: A check-then-insert race allows both callers to observe absence. The authoritative uniqueness constraint or conditional insert serializes the claim and gives one winner.
